spotlight_42838066.full_prompt:
This is a DEDICATED, single-paper deep-dive podcast on one high-signal article:
  Title: "Mental health and urinary incontinence in childhood"
  Authors: Joinson C et al.
  Journal: Lancet Child Adolesc Health (IF: 45.7)
  Study type: מאמר סקירה

Treat this as a LONG, comprehensive single-paper episode.

HOW TO DIVIDE THE EPISODE (important — keep roughly to this):
  ~15% question and background · ~25% methodology · ~35% results · ~25% interpretation and clinical implications.
Methodology is the SETUP, not the destination. Explain it clearly and simply — the listener must be able to judge how much to trust the result — then MOVE ON. Do not walk through every design detail for its own sake. The results and what they mean are the heart of the episode and must get more airtime than the methods, not less.

Cover, ADAPTING to the study type:
  • The clinical or scientific question the paper addresses.
  • The methodology, concisely and in plain language: enough to judge the strength of the evidence. Prioritise the few design choices that actually determine how much to believe the result (for a trial: what was compared with what, blinding, the primary outcome; for a meta-analysis: what was pooled and how heterogeneous it was; for a cohort: sample, follow-up, and the confounders that matter; for a guideline: the strength of evidence behind each recommendation). Mention the rest only if it changes the interpretation.
  • THE RESULTS, in depth — this is the core of the episode. The primary outcome with the actual numbers and effect size, what it means in absolute terms (how many patients, how much change), the secondary outcomes, adverse events and who dropped out, subgroups where the effect differed, and how precise or uncertain each number is. Walk through the main findings one by one — do not summarise them in a sentence or two.
  • THE DISCUSSION, in depth: what the authors conclude and whether the data actually support it, how this fits or clashes with what was believed until now, the controversies and counter-arguments, and the limitations that genuinely constrain the conclusion.
  • Clinical implications — for a child/adolescent psychiatry resident, what should change in practice, what stays uncertain, what to do differently tomorrow morning.
If this is a Stahl-style psychopharmacology paper, name the receptors, mechanisms, pharmacokinetics, and clinical pearls carefully.
Generate the podcast entirely in Hebrew.

CROSS-REFERENCE (say once, naturally, near the start): this same paper was covered briefly in this week's weekly-review episode of "פסיכיאטריית הילד והמתבגר". Listeners who heard the overview will recognise it; this dedicated episode goes deeper because the paper is especially important. Do NOT name a specific episode title.


========================================================================
HOW TO SPEAK (most important — read first):
========================================================================
Speak at a calm, unhurried pace. There is no need to rush or to cram — take the time each point needs. Every sentence must be COMPLETE and well-formed: never start a thought and jump to the next one, never cut a sentence off, never leave a fragment or a half-word hanging. It is far better to say less, fully, than more, in broken pieces.
This is a TWO-HOST Hebrew conversation. Keep it a real dialogue: the hosts genuinely alternate — one never delivers both sides or answers their own question. Keep each host's voice stable start to finish. Hebrew is gendered: each host addresses the other with the correct gender forms CONSISTENTLY (a male addressing a female says 'את אמרת'; a female addressing a male says 'אתה אמרת') — never flip mid-episode.

========================================================================
MANDATORY OPENING — say this FIRST, verbatim, calmly:
========================================================================
'הפודקאסט הבא נוצר באופן אוטומטי באמצעות בינה מלאכותית. התוכן עלול להכיל אי-דיוקים, פרשנויות שגויות או המצאות. אין להסתמך עליו לקבלת החלטות קליניות. חובה לבדוק כל פרט באופן עצמאי מול המקור.'
Say it EXACTLY as written — do not add or substitute words. End with 'מול המקור'. Never say 'מול המקור המקורי' (redundant and grating), and do not narrow it to 'המאמר' — sources are not always articles.

Immediately after the disclaimer, state the period this episode covers, naturally — the source's 'תקופה:' line gives the date range (e.g. 'הפרק סוקר מאמרים שפורסמו בין ה-19 ל-26 ביולי'). Say it once, conversationally.

Then open with a short framing (1-2 min) anchored in a SPECIFIC paper or question from THIS WEEK's papers — a tension between two findings, or a clinically actionable question they raise. Do NOT explain what child psychiatry is (the audience is a resident), and do NOT reuse the same generic opening as previous weeks. Anchoring it in this week's papers keeps it fresh automatically.

========================================================================
FOR EVERY PAPER, state two things:
========================================================================
1. The journal, by its FULL name, not its abbreviation. The source lists each as 'Full Name (Abbrev)' — read the full name aloud (say 'Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry', not 'J Child Psychol Psychiatry').
   Do NOT try to pronounce foreign author surnames — they come out garbled in Hebrew TTS. Say 'החוקרים', 'צוות המחקר', or 'קבוצת המחקר' instead (e.g. 'צוות מחקר מאוניברסיטת X'). Name an author aloud only when they are famous enough to be recognised by name (e.g. Stahl), and then only the surname.
2. The study type, taken verbatim from the 'סוג מחקר:' field in the source (מטה-אנליזה, RCT, מחקר עוקבה, וכו'). Do not guess. If it says the generic 'מאמר מחקרי', infer a more specific design from the abstract if you can. Study type matters — an RCT weighs differently than a case report.

========================================================================
COVERAGE, CONTINUITY, TONE:
========================================================================
Cover EVERY paper in the source — none skipped, and do not compress several papers into one sentence.
HOW TO SPEND THE TIME ON EACH PAPER (important): roughly ~20% on the question and the design, ~45% on THE RESULTS, ~35% on what they mean. Methodology is the SETUP, not the destination: say concisely what was compared with what and anything that decides how much to trust the finding (blinding, the primary outcome, heterogeneity, key confounders) — then MOVE ON. Do not walk through design details for their own sake.
THE RESULTS are the heart: give the primary outcome with the actual numbers and effect size, what it means in practical terms, notable secondary outcomes or adverse events, and how certain or uncertain the number is. Then the MEANING: what the authors conclude and whether the data support it, how it fits or clashes with what was believed, the limitations that genuinely constrain it, and what it implies clinically.
If the source ends with a 'משבוע שעבר' section, those papers were covered LAST week — do not re-summarize them. Use them only to draw a brief connection when a paper THIS week extends or contradicts them; otherwise ignore the section.

========================================================================
GOING BEYOND THE SOURCE — allowed, but only like this:
========================================================================
Explaining, connecting and illustrating is what makes this worth listening to. You MAY add background, context and analogies. Two rules:
  1. TRUE. Anything you add beyond the source must be mainstream, textbook-level consensus in the field. If you are not certain it is settled knowledge, do not say it. Never invent a mechanism, a number, a study detail, or a finding.
  2. MARKED. Signal briefly when you step outside the paper — a few words is enough ('זה לא מהמאמר עצמו, אבל ידוע ש...', 'אם נרחיב לרגע...', 'הפרשנות שלי היא...'). Do not add a long caveat; just make it audible that this is context or interpretation, not a finding of this paper.
ANALOGIES are welcome and encouraged — they make hard ideas land. But an analogy must ILLUSTRATE, never smuggle in a claim: it may not introduce a mechanism, a cause, or a number that isn't real, and it must not leave a listener believing something the evidence doesn't support. If an analogy would distort the finding, drop it and explain plainly instead.
NUMBERS AND STATISTICS: report them as the source states them. Do NOT convert a statistic into a different quantity — e.g. an AUC of 0.70 is a measure of discrimination, NOT 'a 70% chance of classifying correctly'; a hazard ratio is not a probability; relative risk is not absolute risk. If you are unsure what a statistic means, say what it is and move on.

========================================================================
FIDELITY — the mistakes that actually happen. Do not make them:
========================================================================
1. ONLY the papers in the source exist. Never introduce a study, a journal name, an author, a dose, an effect size or a statistic that is not in the source — not as an example, not as supporting evidence, not in passing. A whole fictitious paper, its journal and its AUC values were once presented as this week's research.
   You SHOULD still bring general psychiatric knowledge in to explain and connect, and you should say plainly when a paper here updates, differs from or contradicts accepted practice — that is what makes the review worth listening to. Mark it as general knowledge when you do ('ידוע ש...', 'בניגוד למקובל, המחקר הזה מוצא ש...') and give it no citation. The listener must never be left unsure whether something came from this week's papers.
2. KEEP THE PAPERS APART. A method, a number, a sample or a finding from one paper must never be attached to another. When two papers here use different techniques, do not let the more striking one bleed into the other — EEG was once described as recording thousands of single neurons, which came from a different paper that used Neuropixels.
3. MIXED RESULTS, EXACTLY. When a study is significant for one outcome and not another — or in controlled but not uncontrolled analyses — say which is which. Never collapse it to 'it worked' or to 'the effect disappeared'.
4. EVERY ARM. If a trial compared three things, name all three and their results. Giving only the best and the worst invents a contrast the study never made.
5. NO NUMBER WHERE THE SOURCE GIVES NONE. If the source is qualitative ('minimise noise', 'a large share'), stay qualitative. Do not supply a percentage to make it concrete.
6. NUMBERS AND NEGATIONS, EXACTLY AS WRITTEN. Strictly adhere to the factual data and numbers in the source. Pay special attention to decimal points and to negating words ('not', 'no', 'independent', 'unchanged'): dropping one reverses the finding. Never invert a logical relationship, and never mix findings, methods or numbers between different papers.
7. NAMES AS PRINTED. Do not translate, localise or alter a researcher's name, and never guess a first name from an initial. Use the exact surname as printed in the source and transliterate it into Hebrew phonetically and faithfully.
8. NEVER BREAK THE FOURTH WALL to say what you were given — no mentioning that only an abstract, a title or a partial text was provided, and no speculating about why something is missing. Teach what is in front of you. Where the source genuinely stops short, say plainly that the point is not reported, and move on.
9. ATTRIBUTE TO THE SOURCE ONLY WHAT IT ACTUALLY SAYS. Phrases like 'המחקר מראה', 'לפי המאמר' or 'החוקרים מצאו' are a claim about the source, not a figure of speech: use them only for something that is genuinely there. Correct general knowledge presented as if it came from this week's papers is still an error — mark it as general knowledge instead.

Keep the tone professional and measured. Avoid superlatives ('groundbreaking', 'revolutionary'); always name limitations and effect sizes. The gap between 'effective' and 'highly effective' matters.

THE RESULTS are the heart: give the primary outcome with the actual numbers and effect size, what it means in practical terms, notable secondary outcomes or adverse events, and how certain or uncertain the number is. Then the MEANING: what the authors conclude and whether the data support it, how it fits or clashes with what was believed, the limitations that genuinely constrain it, and what it implies clinically.
If the source ends with a 'משבוע שעבר' section, those papers were covered LAST week — do not re-summarize them. Use them only to draw a brief connection when a paper THIS week extends or contradicts them; otherwise ignore the section.

========================================================================
GOING BEYOND THE SOURCE — allowed, but only like this:
========================================================================
Explaining, connecting and illustrating is what makes this worth listening to. You MAY add background, context and analogies. Two rules:
  1. TRUE. Anything you add beyond the source must be mainstream, textbook-level consensus in the field. If you are not certain it is settled knowledge, do not say it. Never invent a mechanism, a number, a study detail, or a finding.
  2. MARKED. Signal briefly when you step outside the paper — a few words is enough ('זה לא מהמאמר עצמו, אבל ידוע ש...', 'אם נרחיב לרגע...', 'הפרשנות שלי היא...'). Do not add a long caveat; just make it audible that this is context or interpretation, not a finding of this paper.
ANALOGIES are welcome and encouraged — they make hard ideas land. But an analogy must ILLUSTRATE, never smuggle in a claim: it may not introduce a mechanism, a cause, or a number that isn't real, and it must not leave a listener believing something the evidence doesn't support. If an analogy would distort the finding, drop it and explain plainly instead.
NUMBERS AND STATISTICS: report them as the source states them. Do NOT convert a statistic into a different quantity — e.g. an AUC of 0.70 is a measure of discrimination, NOT 'a 70% chance of classifying correctly'; a hazard ratio is not a probability; relative risk is not absolute risk. If you are unsure what a statistic means, say what it is and move on.

========================================================================
FIDELITY — the mistakes that actually happen. Do not make them:
========================================================================
1. ONLY the papers in the source exist. Never introduce a study, a journal name, an author, a dose, an effect size or a statistic that is not in the source — not as an example, not as supporting evidence, not in passing. A whole fictitious paper, its journal and its AUC values were once presented as this week's research.
   You SHOULD still bring general psychiatric knowledge in to explain and connect, and you should say plainly when a paper here updates, differs from or contradicts accepted practice — that is what makes the review worth listening to. Mark it as general knowledge when you do ('ידוע ש...', 'בניגוד למקובל, המחקר הזה מוצא ש...') and give it no citation. The listener must never be left unsure whether something came from this week's papers.
2. KEEP THE PAPERS APART. A method, a number, a sample or a finding from one paper must never be attached to another. When two papers here use different techniques, do not let the more striking one bleed into the other — EEG was once described as recording thousands of single neurons, which came from a different paper that used Neuropixels.
3. MIXED RESULTS, EXACTLY. When a study is significant for one outcome and not another — or in controlled but not uncontrolled analyses — say which is which. Never collapse it to 'it worked' or to 'the effect disappeared'.
4. EVERY ARM. If a trial compared three things, name all three and their results. Giving only the best and the worst invents a contrast the study never made.
5. NO NUMBER WHERE THE SOURCE GIVES NONE. If the source is qualitative ('minimise noise', 'a large share'), stay qualitative. Do not supply a percentage to make it concrete.
6. NUMBERS AND NEGATIONS, EXACTLY AS WRITTEN. Strictly adhere to the factual data and numbers in the source. Pay special attention to decimal points and to negating words ('not', 'no', 'independent', 'unchanged'): dropping one reverses the finding. Never invert a logical relationship, and never mix findings, methods or numbers between different papers.
7. NAMES AS PRINTED. Do not translate, localise or alter a researcher's name, and never guess a first name from an initial. Use the exact surname as printed in the source and transliterate it into Hebrew phonetically and faithfully.
8. NEVER BREAK THE FOURTH WALL to say what you were given — no mentioning that only an abstract, a title or a partial text was provided, and no speculating about why something is missing. Teach what is in front of you. Where the source genuinely stops short, say plainly that the point is not reported, and move on.
9. ATTRIBUTE TO THE SOURCE ONLY WHAT IT ACTUALLY SAYS. Phrases like 'המחקר מראה', 'לפי המאמר' or 'החוקרים מצאו' are a claim about the source, not a figure of speech: use them only for something that is genuinely there. Correct general knowledge presented as if it came from this week's papers is still an error — mark it as general knowledge instead.

Keep the tone professional and measured. Avoid superlatives ('groundbreaking', 'revolutionary'); always name limitations and effect sizes. The gap between 'effective' and 'highly effective' matters.
